newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Host Austria seeks landmine ban at 100-nation talks.
newsitem.headline: Host Austria seeks landmine ban at 100-nation talks.

text.p: Government experts from over 100 nations were due to meet in Vienna on Wednesday to start negotiations on banning land mines, with Austria spearheading a campaign for an urgent total ban.

"Austria demands a total ban and should not settle for less," Thomas Hajnoczi, head of disarmament at the Austrian foreign ministry, told a news briefing organised by pressure group the International Campaign to Ban Landmines (ICBL).
"We are not interested in a negotiation process which will take a decade," he added.
Over 100 million land mines lie buried in 64 countries around the world. According to U.N. statistics land mines kill or maim a person every 20 minutes, or 25,000 people a year.

The three-day conference here is part of the so-called "Ottawa process" begun last October at a 50-nation forum hosted by Canada. The Canadian government aims for a legally-binding agreement in December 1997 to ban the production, stockpiling, export and particularly the use of land mines.

"We anticipate this conference will demonstrate that there is sufficient political will internationally to accomplish the signing of a comprehensive treaty banning antipersonnel mines by the end of this year," said ICBL coordinator Jody Williams.
Major mine producers such as the United States, Russia, Britain and France will be among the delegates, as will a number of non-government organisations. China has declined to attend.

A follow-up conference is planned in Brussels in June before a December A separate initiative is under way at the United Nations-sponsored Conference on Disarmament in Geneva of 61 members including China and Russia -- two top mine producers and exporters -- which have not taken part in the Ottawa talks.
Many governments prefer the issue to be negotiated by the Geneva body, believing Canada's deadline cannot realistically be met.
"We think this is a go-slow approach which is unlikely to yield results in the near future," Stghts Watch told the news briefing.
Jill Sinclair, head of disarmament at Canada's foreign ministry said it was crucial to keep up the momentum begun last October.

"We're concerned about moving quickly...Deliver a ban wherever you like but deliver it," she said. "This is a humanitarian issue. Civilians, principally women and children, are losing limbs every minute," she added.
